(CNN) -- Every dog has his day, but Sir Lancelot -- or at least his carbon copy -- has a second one. Edgar and Nina Otto show off 10-week-old Lancey, a clone of "the most human of any dog we've ever had." A Boca Raton, Florida, couple paid a California firm $155,000 to clone their beloved Labrador retriever, who died from cancer a year ago. The clone, a 10-week-old puppy dubbed Lancey, was hand-delivered to them earlier this week by Lou Hawthorne, chairman of BioArts International, a biotechnology company. "One minute with Lancey and you know he's special. He's both extremely aware and very sweet," Hawthorne said in a BioArts statement. Edgar and Nina Otto said they began thinking about cloning Sir Lancelot about five years ago. "I said 'Well, you know, it wouldn't hurt to have his DNA frozen,' and that's what we did," Nina Otto told CNN affiliate WPBF. The Ottos were one of five families to bid and win a BioArts auction for a chance to clone their family dog, according to a BioArts statement. Lancey is the world's first commercially cloned dog, the company said; the Ottos are the first of six current clients to receive their clone. Sir Lancelot's DNA sample was sent to the Sooam Biotech Research Foundation in Seoul, South Korea, which provides cloning services to BioArts. Researchers there put the DNA into an egg, and Lancey was born November 18, according to BioArts. The Ottos said they have had many beloved dogs over the years -- and have nine others currently -- but maintain Sir Lancelot was special. "Sir Lancelot was the most human of any dog we've ever had," Edgar Otto said in the BioArts statement. "He was a prince among dogs." In an interview with WPBF, Edgar Otto said Sir Lancelot "was a very, very, very special dog to us. And we've given a lot more to the Humane Society than we've ever spent on this project."  Watch the Ottos talk about Lancelot and Lancey » . For its part, the Humane Society of the United States says it's against the commercial cloning of animals. "Given the current pet overpopulation problem, which costs millions of animals their lives and millions in public tax dollars each year, the cloning of pets has no social value and in fact may lead to increased animal suffering," the organization said on its Web site. "For those looking to replace a lost pet, cloning will not create an animal identical to the one who is gone; cloning cannot replicate an animal's uniqueness. Cloning can only replicate the pet's genetics, which influence but do not determine his physical attributes or personality." The Ottos, however, said replicating Sir Lancelot's genetics is enough for them. Edgar Otto said he realizes Lancey might not be just like their departed dog, but "if he's different, we're not going to love him any less." Edgar Otto is the son of the late Edwin Otto, who was part of the founding of NASCAR and a "motorsports pioneer," according to www.ottomotorsports.com.

Edgar and Nina Otto, a couple from Boca Raton, Florida, paid a California company $155,000 to clone their beloved Labrador retriever, who died of cancer a year ago. “One minute with Lancey and you know he’s special. He’s both extremely aware and very sweet,” Hawthorne said in a BioArts statement.

According to BioArts, the Ottos were one of five families to bid in and win a BioArts auction for the opportunity to clone their family dog. The company said Lancey is the world’s first commercially cloned dog, and that the Ottos are the first of six current clients to receive their clone.

Sir Lancelot’s DNA sample was sent to the Sooam Biotech Research Foundation in Seoul, South Korea, which provides cloning services to BioArts. Researchers there placed the DNA into an egg, and Lancey was born on November 18, according to BioArts.

The Ottos said they have had many beloved dogs over the years — and currently have nine others — but maintain that Sir Lancelot was exceptional.

“Sir Lancelot was the most human of any dog we’ve ever had,” Edgar Otto said in the BioArts statement. “He was a prince among dogs.”

For its part, the Humane Society of the United States says it opposes the commercial cloning of animals.

“Given the current pet overpopulation problem, which costs millions of animals their lives and millions in public tax dollars each year, the cloning of pets has no social value and in fact may lead to increased animal suffering,” the organization said on its website.

A Florida couple has become widely known for taking part in one of the most unusual developments in the pet industry: commercial dog cloning. Edgar and Nina Otto paid BioArts International $155,000 to clone their beloved Labrador retriever, Sir Lancelot, who had died after years as a cherished family companion. Before the dog’s death, the couple had preserved samples of his DNA, hoping that advances in science might one day make it possible to bring back an animal genetically identical to him.

BioArts International, a California-based biotechnology company, arranged the cloning through a South Korean laboratory with experience in canine cloning. Using the preserved genetic material, scientists created an embryo and implanted it into a surrogate dog. The result was a healthy Labrador puppy named Lancey, also known as “Lancelot Encore.” The Ottos described the puppy as a continuation of the dog they had loved, though scientists emphasized that a clone is not a true resurrection. While Lancey shared Sir Lancelot’s DNA, his personality, behavior, and life experiences would still be shaped by environment, training, and chance.

Lancey was promoted as the world’s first commercially cloned dog, marking a major milestone in the growing market for pet cloning. The case attracted international attention because it suggested that cloning, once limited to research laboratories, was becoming a service available to private individuals willing to pay a high price. For grieving pet owners, the idea offered comfort: the possibility of preserving a genetic link to an animal they considered part of the family.

However, the cloning also raised serious ethical questions. Animal-welfare organizations criticized the practice, arguing that cloning can involve failed pregnancies, unhealthy embryos, and the use of multiple surrogate animals. They also questioned whether wealthy owners should spend large sums cloning pets when millions of dogs and cats in shelters need homes. Critics warned that cloning could encourage people to view animals as replaceable products rather than unique living beings.

Supporters of the technology argued that pet cloning is a personal choice and that the science could have broader benefits, including preserving valuable genetics from working dogs, endangered species, or animals with exceptional traits. Still, the birth of Lancey became a symbol of both the promise and controversy surrounding commercial cloning. It showed how far biotechnology had advanced, while also forcing the public to confront difficult questions about grief, animal welfare, and the limits of using science to recreate the past.

counterfactuals.output:
**BOCA RATON, Florida (CNN) —** A Florida couple who lost their beloved Labrador retriever has received what they say is the next best thing to having him back: a cloned puppy created from the dog’s preserved DNA.

Edgar and Nina Otto of Boca Raton paid $155,000 to have their late yellow Labrador, Lancelot, cloned by BioArts International, a California-based biotechnology company that offered the service through an auction called “Best Friends Again.”

The resulting puppy, named **Lancelot Encore**, was born in South Korea and delivered to the Ottos in Florida, where the couple introduced him as a healthy, lively Labrador with a familiar look.

“We are so thrilled,” Nina Otto said, describing the puppy’s arrival as an emotional moment after the loss of the original Lancelot. “He looks just like him.”

Her husband, Edgar Otto, said the couple understood that the puppy would not be the same dog in personality or experience, but they wanted a genetic continuation of a pet they considered part of the family.

“We know he’s not Lancelot,” he said. “But he’s a clone, and he’s got the same DNA. We’re just excited to have him.”

The Ottos had banked tissue from Lancelot years before he died, making the cloning possible. The dog’s genetic material was used to create an embryo, which was implanted in a surrogate mother dog. The puppy was then carried to term and born as part of a collaboration involving BioArts and cloning specialists in South Korea.

BioArts chairman **Lou Hawthorne** said the company’s work was intended for owners with deep attachments to individual animals and the resources to pursue cloning.

“This is not about replacing a pet,” Hawthorne said. “It’s about giving people the opportunity to have a new animal that is genetically identical to one they loved.”

Hawthorne said Lancelot Encore’s birth showed that commercial dog cloning could be done successfully, though he acknowledged that genetics alone do not recreate the original animal.

“A clone is an identical twin born at a later time,” Hawthorne said. “It will have the same genes, but environment and experience will shape who that animal becomes.”

The cloning of dogs has long been considered more difficult than cloning some other mammals because of canine reproductive biology. The first widely recognized cloned dog, an Afghan hound named Snuppy, was born in South Korea in 2005. Since then, the technology has remained expensive, technically demanding and controversial.

Animal-welfare groups sharply criticized the Ottos’ decision and the broader commercialization of pet cloning.

The **Humane Society of the United States** said cloning pets is unnecessary at a time when millions of dogs and cats are euthanized in shelters each year for lack of homes. The organization has also objected to the cloning process itself, arguing that it can require many failed embryos, egg donors and surrogate animals to produce a single surviving clone.

“Pet cloning is a misguided and frivolous use of biotechnology,” the Humane Society said in objections to the practice. “It does nothing to address the tragedy of pet overpopulation, and it raises serious animal-welfare concerns.”

The group said grieving owners should consider adoption rather than paying large sums to create a genetic copy of a deceased pet.

“There are so many wonderful animals in shelters waiting for homes,” the Humane Society said. “Cloning one dog does not bring back the animal who died, and it may contribute to the suffering of others used in the process.”

The Ottos said they are animal lovers and that they did not view cloning as a substitute for adoption or traditional pet ownership. They live with several animals and said their decision was based on their extraordinary attachment to Lancelot.

For them, Lancelot Encore is not a scientific debate but a puppy settling into a new home.

“He’s part of our family now,” Nina Otto said. “That’s what matters to us.”

counterfactuals.output:
(CNN) -- Every dog has his day. For one Florida family, that day arrived in the form of a wriggling yellow Labrador retriever puppy born not by chance, but by cloning.

The puppy, named Lancelot Encore, was created from the DNA of Sir Lancelot, a beloved Labrador owned by Edgar and Nina Otto. The couple had preserved genetic material from their pet before his death, later paying a reported $155,000 to have him cloned through a commercial pet-cloning program.

The result was billed as the world’s first commercially cloned dog — a milestone that thrilled the Ottos and reignited a fierce ethical debate over whether science should be used to replicate companion animals.

Dog cloning is technically difficult. Unlike some other mammals, dogs have complex reproductive cycles that make the process challenging and expensive. Scientists first successfully cloned a dog in 2005, a male Afghan hound named Snuppy, produced by researchers in South Korea. Commercial cloning followed soon after, promising grieving owners the possibility of a genetic twin of a lost pet.

But experts caution that a clone is not a resurrection.

A cloned dog shares the same DNA as the original animal, much like an identical twin born at a different time. Its appearance may be strikingly similar, but personality, behavior and temperament are shaped by environment, training, socialization and experience.

Animal welfare advocates also question the cost behind each successful clone. The process can involve multiple egg donors, surrogate mothers and failed pregnancies. Critics argue that cloning pets diverts attention and money from shelters filled with animals in need of homes.

“People are paying six figures to copy one dog while millions of dogs and cats are euthanized or abandoned,” critics often argue. “That raises serious moral questions.”

Supporters see it differently. To them, cloning is another reproductive technology — unusual, expensive and imperfect, but not inherently unethical if animals are treated humanely. For owners who have formed deep bonds with their pets, the chance to preserve a genetic link can feel priceless.

The debate touches on broader questions about grief, science and the way humans relate to animals. Is cloning a loving tribute, or an attempt to deny loss? Does the technology celebrate the bond between people and pets, or commodify living creatures?

For the Ottos, Lancelot Encore was not simply a scientific achievement. He was a puppy to be fed, trained and loved — similar to the dog they lost, but also an individual in his own right.

As pet cloning becomes more accessible, if still costly, more families may face the same question: when a beloved animal dies, should technology offer a second chance — or should every dog’s day be allowed to end naturally?
